prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing the measurement of time to an accuracy of about one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part configuration B015 (Katori, Ye) that I adopted in round 1; nothing in the exchange changed it, and several arguments strengthened it. The scientific core is a distinct architecture, not a refinement: trapping many neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift of the clock transition while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement, so statistics of many atoms and freedom from Doppler and recoil effects arrive together. A single trapped ion cannot do this, which is why I do not accept that the 2012 prize covers it. The 2005 prize concerned the frequency comb as the tool that counts optical cycles, and a lattice clock is a user of that tool, not an instance of it. The claim has been tested the way a measurement claim should be: several laboratories on several continents, more than one species (Sr, Yb), and direct clock-to-clock comparisons that agree near 1e-18. The credit follows a proposal-and-realisation split that every member who discussed it accepts: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the frontier. If the citation is worded around the lattice concept and the achieved accuracy, and not around combs, clocks in general or the redefinition of the second, I think it is defensible to a field-neutral reader.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. First, the novelty argument depends on the committee accepting the lattice as a separate invention; a member who sees optical frequency standards as one programme honoured in 2005 and 2012 will reasonably find a third prize in the line less compelling. Second, a two-name credit leaves out strong contributors (Lemonde at SYRTE, Lisdat at PTB, Ludlow, Lemke, Bloom, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups), and I cannot show from the supplied record that none of them has a claim equal to Ye's. Third, this is an instrument-driven advance, and Danielsson is right that it is less obviously a discovery of nature than neutrino astronomy or a new class of matter. I weigh that against attribution and maturity, but it is a judgement and not a measurable criterion, and I do not claim it is settled.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B018 first as the strongest condensed-matter case, and says the lattice clock may be read as a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes; he also concedes that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers cannot fit in a three-name credit.
responses.response: Of the chair's questions, his is the one I take most seriously, and my answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a different physical architecture from the single-ion clock and not a refinement of a comb. A citation naming the lattice concept and the accuracy it achieved says that. On B018 I accept his account of the science, and his own concession is the reason I stay with B015: the credit would drop Mele, whose Z2 papers with Kane are foundational, and the choice between Hasan and Xue for the third name is unsettled. I keep B018 as my first alternative and would back it if the committee settled a defensible credit line.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B014 first as a discovery of nature in the plain sense, with a compact Halzen-Karle credit, and himself says B015 should be preferred if clean attribution outweighs breadth of discovery.
responses.response: I agree with how he frames the choice, and I give attribution that weight. The diffuse flux is a real discovery, but the source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is still statistically modest, so a citation limited to the diffuse flux is the defensible one, and two names would then stand for a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND antecedents. I cannot settle that credit from the record. I would not oppose B014 in a later year, and I list it as an alternative, but I do not think this year's committee can argue it is more secure than B015, which he effectively concedes.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a different physical architecture, that the redefinition of the second is an application milestone and not a doubt about the science, and that SYRTE, PTB, NIST and ion groups are not covered by two names; he also keeps B032 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree on the first two points and they are the core of my case. On credit I accept that the objection stands and I do not propose a third name: the only candidate I can justify from the record is a contributor from the Ye group or from SYRTE or PTB, and I cannot show that any of them stands above the others in the way Katori's concept and Ye's performance do. A named third laureate chosen on my memory would be weaker than the clean pair. I still do not support B032, because Cirac and Zoller also appear in B009, and a clock prize does not preempt an ultracold-atom prize later.

responses.point: Lindroth treats B015 as the single-achievement baseline that two-part packages must justify themselves against, and asks whether pairing it with B014 or B030 would give a better balanced prize or only an artificial one.
responses.response: I agree with the baseline and would answer her question against a pairing. The three-person limit forces one of the laureates out of either part: B015 with B014 would drop Katori or Ye, or give B014 a single name, and either result damages the cleanest credit on the shortlist to buy balance. Neither B014 nor B030 has a settled credit or, for B030, a settled mechanism for the superconductivity, and I would not make a good prize weaker to make it more varied. I would keep a single part.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moves to B015 for the independent confirmation by laboratories on several continents and the cleanest attribution, but says B014 is stronger on opening a wholly new observational window.
responses.response: I accept that the independence of the confirmations is established by the inter-laboratory comparisons across institutions and species, and not only by repeated reports from one group, and I would be content for the committee to ask for that data directly before the vote. On his remark about B014 I agree it is stronger as a window on nature. I would answer that the prize rewards the discovery or invention whose originators can be identified, and that is where the lattice clock is ahead. He also asks that Kroll's connection to the Hall laboratory be recorded; I agree it should be, and I see it as background that does not alter the evidence on B015.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a separate invention and not as part of the line honoured in 2005 and 2012; I cannot offer a test beyond the physical argument.
Whether a third name from the lattice-clock community would improve the credit; I cannot find one from the supplied record that I can defend.

Whether the statistical-physics candidate B005 could attract support beyond mine; I no longer put it among my alternatives because the attribution among Evans, Gallavotti-Cohen, Jarzynski and Crooks remains contested.
Whether the Hasan-or-Xue question and the omission of Mele can be settled in a way that makes a topological prize defensible.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My field (statistical physics of complex systems, turbulence, neural networks) is not close to precision atomic physics, and I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or any of the other credited names. My earlier first-place ranking of B005 reflected subject-matter preference, and I have now dropped it from my configuration. I have noted the disclosures by Kroll (a research stay in John Hall's laboratory) and Johansson (WACQT roles) and think the committee should record them, but neither affects my own position.
